title: Move Zeroes: two-pointer compaction.
shortTitle: Move Zeroes: Two-Pointer Compaction Keeping Order
keyPoints: A slow pointer marks where the next non-zero goes; a fast pointer scans every element
The write-and-fill approach copies non-zeros forward in pass 1 and fills zeros in pass 2
The swap variant moves zeros and non-zeros in a single pass, minimizing writes when zeros are rare
Stability (preserving non-zero order) is the core requirement; sorting or two-ends swapping violates it
The algorithm is O(n) time and O(1) space, done entirely in place
This is the same pattern as stable partitioning, reusable for any predicate

s1_definition.oneliner: Write every non-zero to the front with a slow pointer, then pad the rest with zeros: order preserved, no extra array.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Two-pointer compaction** – a slow pointer (insert) and a fast pointer (scan) walk the array together.
- **Write-and-fill** – pass 1 copies non-zeros forward; pass 2 fills the remaining positions with zeros.
- **Swap variant** – on finding a non-zero, swap it with the insert position in one pass.
- **Stability** – non-zero values keep their original relative order.
- **In-place** – only two index variables are used; no extra array is allocated.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya has a list of this month's charges at National Bank of India where cancelled charges show as zero. She wants all real charges pushed to the front in the same order they happened, with the zeros swept to the back. She keeps one finger on the next clean slot and scans with another; every real charge gets written forward, then the leftover slots become zeros.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Move Zeroes rearranges an array so every zero ends up at the back while the non-zero values keep their original order, done in place. I treat it as a same-direction two-pointer compaction: a slow pointer marks the next slot for a non-zero, and a fast pointer scans the entire array. Each time the fast pointer sees a non-zero, I copy it to the slow slot and advance the slow pointer. After the scan, the front holds all non-zeros in order, and I fill the tail with zeros.

The property interviewers test is stability: the non-zero order must not change. The copy approach preserves it naturally because I write non-zeros in the exact order I meet them. Sorting or two-ends swapping would get the zeros in place but fail the ordering requirement.

The in-place constraint is the whole point of the problem. Allocating a second array is trivially correct but disqualifying. I stay within the original array using only two index variables. For money at the National Bank of India, I use `BigDecimal` and check with `signum()` rather than `==`.

The senior-level insights are that this is really a stable partition around a predicate (reusable for any condition), that the write-and-fill version minimizes writes on zero-heavy arrays while the swap version is better on zero-rare arrays, and that skipping self-writes when the pointers coincide reduces memory traffic on large batch processing arrays.

Remember one sentence: a slow pointer collects non-zeros at the front in order, the tail is filled with zeros, and the result is a stable in-place partition in O(n) time with O(1) space.
